scenes.title: Hook
scenes.narration: Here's a question: when an app remembers your name… where does it actually put it?

scenes.title: What is a variable?
scenes.narration: Every program needs to remember things — your score in a game, the items in your cart, the name you just typed in. A variable is how a program remembers. It's a named piece of the computer's memory that holds a value. And as the name suggests, that value can vary — it can change while the program runs. You give it a name, you put something inside, and you can swap that something at any time.

scenes.title: The labeled box analogy
scenes.narration: Think of a variable as a labeled box. The label is the name, and whatever sits inside is the value. A box labeled "score" might hold ten right now. Play one round, and the program takes the ten out and drops in a fifty. Same box, same label — new contents. A constant is a different kind of box. Once you put a value in and shut the lid, it locks. Nobody can swap what's inside. The program can only look at it.

scenes.title: Real code
scenes.narration: Here's what that looks like in real code — this is JavaScript. "Let score equal ten" creates a variable. The word "let" tells the computer: make me a box. "Score" is the label, and ten goes inside. Later we write "score equals fifty" — no "let" this time, because the box already exists. We're simply replacing its contents. Now the constant: "const PI equals 3.14159". "Const" is short for constant, and it works the same way — one name, one value — with one big exception. If you try to change it, the program stops and throws an error. That's not the computer being difficult. That's protection you asked for.

scenes.title: Which one do you use?
scenes.narration: So choosing between them comes down to one question: will this value ever need to change? A score, a countdown, a username someone might edit — those change, so use a variable. The days in a week, a tax rate, your app's name — those should never change, so use a constant. And here's a habit professionals swear by: reach for a constant first, and only switch to a variable when something truly needs to change.

scenes.title: Recap & takeaway
scenes.narration: One line to remember: variables are labeled boxes you can refill; constants are boxes that lock. Name your data, protect what shouldn't change — and you've just learned the first real building block of every program ever written. See you in the next one.
